title: A balance guarded by a private lock

blocks.text: The page's counter protects `count++` with `synchronized`, and prefers a **dedicated, private lock object** to `synchronized` methods, because a method lock is `this`, and any outside code can take `this` too. It also warns that `synchronized (new Object())` protects nothing, since every call gets its own lock.
Write `Balance`, a balance many threads may change:

items: `int update(IntUnaryOperator change)` applies `change` to the balance and returns the new balance. Only one update runs at a time: a second update **waits** until the first has finished.
Code outside the class that does `synchronized (balance) { ... }` must not be able to stall `update`.
If `change` throws, the exception reaches the caller, the balance keeps its old value, and the next update, from any thread, still runs.

rows: another thread holds `synchronized (balance)`; this thread calls `update(x -> x + 1)`

cases.says: Each update applies its change to the balance and returns the new balance.
While one update is running, a second update waits for it instead of running beside it.
Code that synchronizes on the Balance object itself does not block its updates.
A change that throws leaves the balance as it was, and a later update from another thread still runs.

concepts: Only one thread at a time holds an object's intrinsic lock, so a second synchronized update waits for the first.
A private final lock object keeps outside code from taking the lock, which a synchronized method on this cannot.
The intrinsic lock is released when a synchronized block exits, even by an exception.
A lock protects shared state only when every thread uses the same lock object; synchronized (new Object()) protects nothing.
